deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a German-language page of notes on ancient history, apparently taken from a lecture or textbook on the Hellenistic successor states. It continues the account of Seleucus I Nicator begun on f.158 and goes on into the reigns of Antiochus I and Antiochus II. The hand is a fluent Kurrent with Latin script for proper names. From this page alone I cannot attribute it to Gauss with confidence; it could be a student's or family member's notebook bound into the bundle.

Content, in order:
(1) Seleucus and Lysimachus were dissatisfied with the division made after Antigonus's defeat at Ipsus, so war broke out in 282.
(2) Seleucus took Sardes. Lysimachus came out of Thrace, and they met at Curupedion (Corupedium) in Phrygia. Seleucus won and Lysimachus fell ('blieb').
(3) Seleucus took Lysimachus's Asian lands and crossed to Europe, where Ptolemaeus Ceraunus murdered him in 281.
(4) Seleucus's realm stretched from the Indus and Jaxartes to the Mediterranean. It was divided into 72 satrapies, but the government remained despotic.
(5) His son Antiochus I Soter succeeded him, reigning 281–262. He gave up the claims on Macedonia and sought only to keep his Asian lands.
(6) In 279 Antiochus tried to conquer Bithynia. King Nicomedes called in the Gauls who had invaded Greece, and Antiochus defeated them in 275.
(7) The state of Pergamus in Asia now formed ('in Asien' is a marginal insertion).
(8) Antiochus II Theos reigned 262–247. He had a wife Laodice, said to be also his half-sister ('Stiefschwester'), and a full sister Apame. Apame drew him into a war with Ptolemaeus Philadelphus.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. The only numbers are BC dates and reign spans: 281−262 = 19 years and 262−247 = 15 years.
errors: Not mathematical errors but historical imprecisions, judged against modern chronology. Corupedium is now dated 281 BC (early in the year); the war indeed began c. 282.
The reign dates follow an older chronology. Antiochus I is now given 281–261 BC and Antiochus II 261–246 BC, not 281–262 and 262–247.
'vom Indus' overstates the empire: Seleucus ceded the Indus satrapies to Chandragupta c. 305/303 BC.
Nicomedes I's call to the Gauls is usually dated 278/277. The 'Elephant Victory' is dated anywhere from c. 275 to 269, so 275 is plausible but disputed.
Laodice I is usually considered Antiochus II's cousin (daughter of Achaeus). The 'half-sister' claim comes from Polyaenus and is doubtful.
Apama, daughter of Antiochus I, married Magas of Cyrene. The ensuing conflict with Ptolemy II (First/Second Syrian War) is only loosely 'caused' by her; the note's account is simplified.

results.what: Lecture or textbook notes on Seleucid history (Seleucus I to Antiochus II): Corupedium, the murder of Seleucus, the 72 satrapies, the Galatians, the rise of Pergamon, Laodice and Apame
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient sources (Appian, Justin, Polyaenus) via standard early-19th-century history textbooks

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical notes on the Seleucid kings, with no mathematical content. It is routine textbook-level material and may not even be in Gauss's hand.

checkable.asserts: Length of Antiochus I Soter's reign by the dates given on the page (281–262).
Length of Antiochus II Theos's reign by the dates given on the page (262–247).
Interval between the Bithynian campaign (279) and the defeat of the Gauls (275) as dated on the page.

transcription_corrections: 'mittländische Meer' should most likely read 'mittelländische Meer' (Mediterranean), written cramped.
In 'Antiochus' (three occurrences) the writer first wrote 'Antiogus' and added 'ch' above the line. The given transcription normalizes this correctly.
Line 10: 'bis zum' is struck through before 'u. Jaxartes', which is correct. The scribe's intended sense is 'vom Indus u. Jaxartes bis an das mittelländische Meer'.
'in Asien' at the end of the Pergamus line is a marginal or right-side insertion attached by a caret-like mark under 'Pergamus'.
'Curupedion' is the scribe's spelling of Corupedium (Κόρου πεδίον). 'Ceraunus' is for Keraunos; both are as written.
The marginal fragments at the left edge belong to the facing page (f.158 margin), e.g. 'Syrien', 'allein', 'Chrysorrhoas', 'Tigris', 'Stratonice', 'Lysima[chus]'. They are not part of f.159.
